source_uncertainties: Frames were viewed as 2x3 contact sheets scaled to 800x450 per frame, so small terminal text was read at reduced size; every number used in the chapter (link counts 22, 4 and 28; the free table; the modes) was legible in that view. Odd frames f0001-f0063 of W1L3 and even frames f0002-f0094 of W1L4 were viewed.

The lecture's machine is not available. Its creation mask 002, the SELinux context behind the dot after the mode strings, the Red Hat-family inference from the group wheel, and the older procps definition of used in free are inferences from the slides, not statements of the lecture. The inference of the mask 002 holds under three stated conditions (requests 0666 and 0777 by the tools, no default ACL, one mask for the files and TestDir2); the requests of the lecture's tools were not observed. The screens do not show which mechanism set the mask on the lecture's machine.

login.defs: the rule that a default umask of 022 becomes 002 for private user groups is stated in pam_umask(8), option usergroups (man7.org, fetched 2026-10-26), and in the comment in /etc/login.defs of the verification machine (Ubuntu 24.04, shadow 4.13); the man7.org login.defs(5) page documents UMASK as the initial mask used by pam_umask and USERGROUPS_ENAB only for useradd/userdel. On the verification machine the shell prints umask 0022 although USERGROUPS_ENAB is yes and uid equals gid; the cause was not investigated.

GNU Coreutils manual: the web edition at gnu.org returned 403 (anti-bot page) to the fetching client. The chapter cites the Coreutils 9.4 manual as installed with the verification system (info coreutils, read as text); the section numbers 10.1.2, 11.4, 11.5, 27.1, 27.2.6, 27.5 are those of that copy. The web edition may number or word sections differently.

Filesystem Hierarchy Standard 3.0: the HTML edition returned an anti-bot page. The chapter reads the PDF fhs-3.0.pdf (publication date 19 March 2015, 50 PDF pages) and cites sections (Chapter 2, 3.8, 3.18, 5.15), not page numbers.

POSIX pages are the Issue 8 / POSIX.1-2024 edition (pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799). POSIX.1-2017 wording was not compared; sections 4.5 Directory Protection and 4.7 File Access Permissions are numbered as in the 2024 edition.

Linux man-pages were fetched from man7.org on 2026-10-26 (page versions as served then). The kernel of the verification machine is 6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2; other kernels and file systems were not tested.
Ritchie and Thompson (1974) was read in Eric Brewer's electronic recreation. Journal page numbers 366-369 are derived from the page headers of that file (PDF page 1 = journal page 365).

The transcripts with numeric identities 2001, 2002 and 2003 (root_a.sh, root_b.sh; root_a.sh and root_a.out were restored at 21:07 to the content of the original run, and an extra run of a 0604 case is not used; root_b was not edited after its run) were produced by the root account of the WSL guest (wsl -u root) with setpriv, in a scratch directory that was deleted afterwards; no account or group was created. python code_lab.py cannot reproduce them because it runs as the unprivileged user. Standard input was not a terminal in both runs (the chapter says so). Their kernel results equal the model's table (shared_dir_model.py) on all 18 yes/no answers.

access_predicate.py compares the predicate with the kernel on files of the machine that runs it (up to 3000 entries under each of /etc, /var/log, /usr/bin and /home; the walk stops when the budget is used). Under /etc, /var/log and /usr/bin the walk ended before the budget (1516, 206 and 1093 entries examined); only under /home did it stop at 3000. In the run that produced the sample, 2997 entries were in the owner class (all under /home, the test user's own files), 42 in the group class (all under /var/log) and 1946 in the other class; the listing prints only whether each class had at least 20. The counts depend on the machine and change as logs rotate. The owner-class test is exhaustive (512 modes); the order of the group class and the other class was not tested against the kernel (a group member refused under mode 0604 although the other digit grants read is the untested example). The ACL attribute (system.posix_acl_access) was detected through listxattr but its entries were not decoded: getfacl and setfacl are not installed, so the chapter does not say which ACL entry grants the access on the journal files, and the ACL-based repair named in exercise 5 was not tested.

GNU chmod prints 'new permissions are r--r--rw-, not r--r--r--' and exits with status 1 for chmod -w on mode 646 under umask 002. The resulting mode (446) equals the model's result; the reason for the warning was inferred, not read in the source code.

The effect of a set-user-ID program (effective user = file owner) rests on Ritchie and Thompson (1974) and inode(7); no set-user-ID program was run. The mode of /usr/bin/passwd is a fact of the verification machine.

The claim that the 9p-mounted Windows drive does not store Linux modes rests on one test on this machine: chmod 000 on a new file under /mnt/c gave mode 555 in stat. The mount options were not varied.

The directory sizes 4096 and 35 bytes are read from the lecture's slide. The link-count rule (3.1) is verified on this machine's ext4 and assumed for the lecture's file system; link-count conventions of other file systems were not tested.
The chapter does not cover the other parts of the W1L3 outline that the lecture announces (process management, text processing, memory and network commands); they belong to Chapters 2 and 4.

references.title: The UNIX Time-Sharing System (Ritchie and Thompson, CACM 17(7), 1974)
references.supports: A file does not exist within a directory; each directory has at least two entries; no links to directories and none between file system hierarchies; seven protection bits and set-user-ID; i-node fields; link creation and removal by changing the link count
references.page_checked: pp. 366-369 (full text read in the recreated electronic version)

references.title: POSIX.1-2024 Base Definitions, chapter 4 General Concepts
references.supports: 4.5 sticky-bit deletion conditions; 4.7 class-based access rule, privileged processes, additional and alternate mechanisms; 4.8 directed graph

references.title: POSIX.1-2024 chmod
references.supports: owner or privileged may change the mode; symbolic-mode semantics; bits of the creation mask are excluded when who is omitted

references.title: POSIX.1-2024 umask
references.supports: the file mode creation mask utility

references.title: inode(7)
references.supports: inode fields; mode bit values; the owner of a new file is the effective user ID; meaning of the sticky bit on a directory

references.title: path_resolution(7)
references.supports: resolution steps and errors; the three-class permission rule (owner, then group or supplementary group, then other)

references.title: credentials(7)
references.supports: effective and supplementary IDs are used for file permission checks

references.title: open(2)
references.supports: O_TRUNC, O_APPEND; mode and ~umask; the group of a new file depends on set-group-ID of the parent directory; EACCES for creation

references.title: mkdir(2)
references.supports: mode & ~umask & 0777; owner and group of a new directory; set-group-ID inheritance; EEXIST, EACCES

references.title: rmdir(2), link(2), unlink(2), rename(2)
references.supports: ENOTEMPTY; EPERM for directories; EXDEV across file systems; unlink deletes a name, and the file when the last link and last descriptor are gone; sticky-bit conditions; EACCES without write permission on the containing directory
references.page_checked: DESCRIPTION and ERRORS of each page

references.title: symlink(7)
references.supports: permissions of a symbolic link are not used and are always 0777 on Linux
references.page_checked: section on ownership, permissions and timestamps

references.title: chmod(2) and chown(2)
references.supports: only a privileged process may change the owner; the owner may change the group to one of the owner's groups; set-user-ID and set-group-ID cleared on a change by an unprivileged user; chmod needs the owner or a privileged process

references.title: free(1) (procps-ng)
references.supports: used is calculated as total - available

references.title: login.defs(5) and /etc/login.defs of the verification machine
references.supports: UMASK is the initial file mode creation mask used by pam_umask (default 022); the comment in /etc/login.defs states that USERGROUPS_ENAB yes turns 022 into 002 for private user groups
references.page_checked: UMASK and USERGROUPS_ENAB entries of the man page; comment lines 134-146 of /etc/login.defs

references.title: pam_umask(8)
references.supports: option usergroups: if the user is not root and the username equals the primary group name, the umask group bits are set equal to the owner bits (022 becomes 002, 077 becomes 007)

references.title: Filesystem Hierarchy Standard 3.0
references.supports: shareable/static distinction; /home is site-specific; /tmp is not preserved; /var/tmp is preserved
